name: Money Laundering Networks
title: Money Laundering Networks
answer: Money laundering networks are the chains of accounts, shell companies, intermediaries and informal value transfer channels used to move criminal proceeds so their origin is obscured. In fraud detection and forensics the term covers both the physical and legal structures, such as layered corporate ownership and trade based schemes, and the transaction patterns those structures leave in bank, payment and crypto records. The work sits between financial crime compliance, audit and data analysis, and it treats a network as a graph of entities and transfers rather than a list of isolated suspicious payments. The aim is to reconstruct how value moved, who controlled each hop and where the proceeds surfaced.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Money laundering networks are the chains of accounts, shell companies, intermediaries and informal value transfer channels used to move criminal proceeds so their origin is obscured. In fraud detection and forensics the term covers both the physical and legal structures, such as layered corporate ownership and trade based schemes, and the transaction patterns those structures leave in bank, payment and crypto records. The work sits between financial crime compliance, audit and data analysis, and it treats a network as a graph of entities and transfers rather than a list of isolated suspicious payments. The aim is to reconstruct how value moved, who controlled each hop and where the proceeds surfaced.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is transaction and reference data: payment messages, account and counterparty records, corporate registry filings, sanctions and politically exposed person lists, and increasingly wallet and exchange data for crypto flows. These arrive from core banking systems, case management platforms and third party screening providers, often through batch extracts or APIs, and are loaded into a graph store or a relational warehouse with a graph layer on top. Entity resolution tooling links names, addresses and identifiers that refer to the same person or company across sources, because the same beneficial owner may appear under several spellings. Analysts work in link analysis and case tools, and the pipeline usually keeps an audit trail of every query and match for later review.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start from alerts or referrals and build a graph of accounts, owners and transfers, then apply rules for structuring, rapid pass through and round amounts alongside statistical and machine learning models that score subgraphs for risk. Network analytics such as centrality, community detection and path finding help separate ordinary commercial traffic from layering, and temporal analysis shows whether funds moved in coordinated bursts. Investigators corroborate the pattern with documents, corporate records and, where relevant, open source material before drawing conclusions. Findings are written up as a narrative of the flow with supporting exhibits, and the same graph can be queried again when new entities or alerts appear.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: This work sits under anti money laundering and counter terrorist financing obligations, sanctions regimes, data protection law and reporting duties to a financial intelligence unit, and the rules differ by jurisdiction. Suspicious activity reports carry legal protections but also strict confidentiality, so access to case data is limited and logged. Provenance matters: every entity link, model score and document needs a source and a version, because decisions may be reviewed by regulators, auditors or courts. False positives impose real costs on innocent customers, so thresholds and overrides are documented and reviewed. Nothing here is legal advice, and specific obligations depend on the institution and the country.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward shared intelligence and graph native tooling, with consortium data and privacy preserving techniques used to spot networks that no single institution can see alone. Regulators are asking for more explainable models and clearer audit trails, which pushes teams away from opaque scoring toward traceable features and documented reasoning. Crypto and instant payment rails keep expanding the data surface, and real time monitoring is replacing periodic review in many shops. The hard problems that remain are entity resolution across borders, uneven data quality and the tension between sharing what is known and protecting privacy.
